# Introduction
"Seasonality is the periodic and largely repetitive pattern that is observed in time series
data over the course of a year."
Seasonality is a characteristic of many observed time series [see for example the series in,@feng1999kernel;@feng2013seasonal]. It is a pattern that repeats  Furthermore, seasonal patterns can be complex due to slow changes in the pattern over time, as for example found by @hylleberg1993seasonality for macroeconomic time series.

Methods for decomposing seasonal time series are numerous and range from purely parametric approaches, such as OLS (ordinary least squares), over nonparametric ideas, like MA (moving averages), to (almost) fully automated programs, for example BV4.1 [Berlin Procedure 4.1,@speth2004komponentenzerlegung]. The latter is a decomposition method often used by the Federal Statistical Office of Germany alongside other internationally established methods, e.g. X-12-ARIMA [@david1998x12arima].

Recently

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(deseats)
```

# The implemented algorithm

## Locally weighted regression for trend and seasonality

Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Assume a time series $\{Y_t\}_{t\in\{1,\dots,n\}}$ that follows
\begin{equation}
Y_t = M(x_t) + S(x_t) + \varepsilon_t,
\end{equation}
where $x_t = t/n$, $M(x_t)$ is a smooth and deterministic trend function, $S(x_t)$ is a slowly changing seasonal component with seasonal period $p$, and $\varepsilon_t$ is an error component with $E(\varepsilon_t) = 0$, whose elements admit short-range dependence. Let $\{y_t\}_{t\in\{1,\dots,n\}}$ be a realization of the time series $\{Y_t\}$.

# Application

A simple application of the `deseats` package is the automatic decomposition of a seasonal time series with locally weighted regression via the `deseats()` function. Its usage will be shown using the implemented dataset `CONSUMPTION`, which contains data on the quarterly real final consumption expenditures from the third quarter of 1959 to the fourth quarter in 2019. The unit is thousands of domestic currency. Originally, the dataset was obtained from the website of the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. In more detail, the decomposition will be shown for the log-transformed series, as its variation appears to be more stable and therefore the log-transformed series more suitable for an additive component model, as can be seen in Figure ???.

```{r}
L_CONSUMPTION <- log(CONSUMPTION)
plot(cbind(CONSUMPTION, L_CONSUMPTION), xlab = "Year", 
     main = "The original and the log-transformed series")
```


## Setting general smoothing parameters

At first, the general smoothing parameters, such as the second-order kernel function used for weighting, have to be specified using `set_options()`. Its arguments are:
- `order_poly`: the order of local polynomial for the trend,

- `season`: the seasonal period of the series to analyze,

- `kernel_fun`: the kernel function to use for weighting,

- `bwidth`: the relative bandwidth to consider, and

- `boundary_method`: an indicator for the boundary method to use for the bandwidth.

If the provided time series to analyze is a time series object of class `"ts"`, `season` can be left at its default `NA`, as the seasonal period will then be set automatically. Moreover, the default `bwidth = NA` will lead to an automatic bandwidth selection. `order_poly` must be set to either `1` or `3`, while `3` is the suggested choice for most application, and for kernel_fun, only the options `"uniform"`, `"epanechnikov"`, `"bisquare"` and `"triweight"` are available, indicating the corresponding kernel function with the same name. Ultimately, `boundary_method` has the two options `"extend"` and `"shorten"`, where `"extend"` is the preferred setting, as the boundary bandwidths are then extended towards the interior of the series.

If no bandwidth is provided, the algorithm described in Section ??? is called to find an optimal bandwidth. Before the bandwidth selection and the actual decomposition, it is required to set the general parameters for the locally weighted regression using `set_options()`. By default, its argument `bwidth` is set to `NA`, which later on triggers the automatic bandwidth selection in `deseats()`.

In the given scenario, we mainly use default settings and only use the adjustment `order_poly = 3`.
```{r}
opts <- set_options(order_poly = 3)
opts
```

## Decompose a time series

Now that the smoothing options have been set, the actual decomposition can be conducted. For this purpose, the function `deseats()` is called with the time series object being its first argument and the smoothing options being the second one.

```{r}
decomp <- deseats(L_CONSUMPTION, smoothing_options = opts)
decomp
```

The bandwidth 0.1766 was selected automatically by the package's own algorithm for locally weighted regression and immediately implemented. If a selected bandwidth is not suitable, it is suggested to try other settings for the argument `inflation_rate` first. If `order_poly = 1` in the smoothing options, it is automatically set to `inflation_rate = "optimal"`, while the default `inflation_rate = "naive"` is implemented for `order_poly = 3`. These settings are suggested and have shown suitable results in most cases. However, manual settings of `inflation_rate = "optimal"` and `inflation_rate = "naive"` are also possible regardless of the choice of `order_poly` and may lead to different results depending on the time series at hand. Other adjustments for the bandwidth selection algorithm may include the part of observations to omit at each boundary (argument `drop`) and the starting bandwidth (argument `bwidth_start`) among others. For a full overview, we refer the reader to the documentation of the function `deseats()`.

## Visualization of results

After a decomposition has been conducted, the results can be visualized using `plot()` (in the base R framework) and `autoplot()` (in the `ggplot2` framework). There is a list of various plots to create from the decomposition results. The plot can be selected either interactively in the R console or in the function call by setting the `which` argument. A list of the available plots is provided in the documentation of these methods.

```{r}
plot(decomp, which = 1, xlab = "Year")
```
```{r, fig.height = 5}
plot(decomp, which = 5, xlab = "Year")
```

According to Figure ???, the decomposition is suitable. The trend follows the overall level of the time series and also the seasonal pattern, which changes slowly over time, is estimated adequately. The displayed residuals in Figure ??? are approximately stationary and could be analyzed in further steps. Depending on what the goal of the analysis is, we proceed either with an analysis of the residuals or with a simple deseasonalization of the original time series.

### Deseasonalization

First, we obtain the deseasonalized version of the log-transformed time series using `deseasonalize()`.

```{r}
L_DEAS <- deseasonalize(decomp)
ts.plot(L_CONSUMPTION, L_DEAS, xlab = "Year", col = 1:2, lwd = 1:2,
        main = "The deseasonalized log-series")
```

Afterwards, the deseasonalized log-series is retransformed. This step can be omitted for series, which did not need an initial log-transformation.

```{r}
DEAS <- exp(L_DEAS)
ts.plot(CONSUMPTION, DEAS, xlab = "Year", col = 1:2, lwd = 1:2,
        main = "The deseasonalized series")
```

The seasonally adjusted series (shown in red in Figure ???) is a suitable deseasonalized representation of the original time series. It is observable that the seasonal pattern has been removed from the original series, while random fluctuations around the trend are still present in the seasonally adjusted series.

### Residual analysis

```{r, fig.height = 5}
acf(residuals(decomp), main = "ACF of the stationarized series")
```

In Figure ???, the ACF of the both detrended and deseasonalized series indicates that there is significant autocorrelation in the residuals. Instead of fitting an ARMA model to the residuals, we call `s_semiarma()`, which is a wrapper for `deseats()`. First, it repeats the decomposition, before then fitting an ARMA model with orders selected by the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) to the residuals. This way, the result is an object that contains all the information of the nonparametric as well as the parametric parts of the model.

```{r}
model <- s_semiarma(L_CONSUMPTION, set_options(order_poly = 3))
model
```

The AR(2) model
$$\varepsilon_t = 0.5240 \varepsilon_{t-1} + 0.2090 \varepsilon_{t-2} + \eta_t$$
is selected for the residuals.

### Forecasting

Once a S-Semi-ARMA model has been fitted to a time series, we can produce forecasts. Forecasting intervals are available either via the normality assumption or via a bootstrap. First, the ARMA residuals need to be checked for normality. We can do this by considering a Jarque-Bera test, which can be implemented through `tseries::jarque.bera.test()`.

```{r}
tseries::jarque.bera.test(model@par_model$residuals)
```

The $p$-value of the test is clearly larger than 0.05, which indicates that the null hypothesis of normality cannot be rejected. Therefore, when calling `predict.s_semiarma()`, we can leave the argument `method` at its default value `"norm"`. Alternatively, a bootstrap can be implemented by setting `method = "boot"`. By specifying `expo = TRUE`, results are exponentiated in the end as a means of retransformation.

```{r}
fc <- predict(model, n.ahead = 12, expo = TRUE)
plot(fc, xlab = "Year", main = "Forecasting results")
```
